intro: To export Google Sheets as PDF on a Mac, open the spreadsheet at sheets.google.com in Chrome, Safari, or Firefox, then choose File > Print. Pick Workbook, Current sheet, or Selected cells, then click Next, and Chrome asks you to click Print before the file saves.
tldr: Open the spreadsheet at sheets.google.com in Chrome, Safari, or Firefox, then choose File > Print.
Pick Workbook, Current sheet, or Selected cells, then click Next.
In Chrome, click Print in the window that appears. Safari and Firefox download the PDF automatically.
Set paper size, orientation, and margins before you export, then check the preview.
If Download or Print is greyed out, the file owner has limited your access.

blocks.text: How Google Sheets exports to PDF on a Mac

Google Sheets does not have a Mac app. You open it in a browser at sheets.google.com, and the PDF export runs from that browser tab. Chrome, Safari, and Firefox all work, and the steps below apply to each of them.

Google's help pages for Sheets do not list a version number or a last updated date. That means menu labels can change without warning. If a label on your screen looks different from this guide, match the words you see and keep the same order of clicks.
Before you start: browser, access, and the Chrome install option

Pick the browser you already use. Chrome opens a Print window and waits for you to click Print before it saves the file. Safari and Firefox download the PDF automatically once you click Next, so there is no second window to confirm.

Access matters as much as the browser. If you are an Editor or the Owner, you can run the export. If you are a Viewer, the owner may have switched off downloading and printing for your role. The access section below explains that case.

Chrome can also install Sheets as an app on your Mac. Open the spreadsheet, click the More menu in Chrome, then choose Cast, save, and share > Install page as app. You can manage installed apps at chrome://apps. The installed app still runs the web version of Sheets, so the export steps stay the same.

blocks.title: Menus can change
blocks.text: Google's help pages show no version or last updated date. Labels such as Print, Download, and Next may move or be renamed. Read each menu before you click.
Export one sheet, the whole workbook, or selected cells

The Print window lets you choose the scope under sheet options. Workbook prints every sheet tab in the file. Current sheet prints only the tab you have open. Selected cells prints only the range you highlighted before you opened Print.

rows: Every sheet tab in the file, in tab order
You need the full file as one PDF

blocks.caption: Print scope options under sheet options in File > Print.

blocks.text: Selected cells is the option people miss most. Select the range first, then open File > Print, so the option matches your highlight. If you open the Print window first and select cells afterward, the range can be wrong. Look at the preview each time you change the scope.

A common case is a workbook with a summary tab and several data tabs. Choose Current sheet while the summary tab is open, then switch to each data tab and export it in turn. Each export becomes its own PDF, so give the files clear names.
Set paper size, orientation, and margins before you export

The print settings panel lists Paper size, Orientation, and Margins. Paper size includes a Custom size option for unusual page shapes. Orientation switches between Portrait and a sideways option. Pick the sideways option for tables that run across the page, and Portrait for long, narrow lists.

Margins offer preset values. Choose Custom if you want to type your own numbers. Narrower margins give a wide table more room, but very narrow margins can clip text near the edge of the paper, so check the preview.

Headers & footers adds text at the top and bottom of each page. Edit custom fields opens the place where you build that text. Keep footers short, because a long footer takes space away from the table on every page.
Keep column headers on every PDF page

A long table can run onto a second page without its header row. The fix has two parts. Freeze the top row in the sheet, then open File > Print and turn on Repeat frozen rows or columns. The freeze has to happen first, because the print setting only repeats rows you have frozen.

For the freeze steps, see [how to freeze the top row in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/freeze-the-top-row-in-google-sheets). If the first column holds names or IDs, freeze that column too, and turn on the same repeat option for columns.
Control where pages break

Custom page breaks sit inside the print settings. Drag the break lines to the rows where you want a new page to start, then select Confirm breaks. This keeps related rows together, such as every line for one customer or one property.

A break in one place can push other lines onto new pages, so check the preview after each change. The preview is the only place to see where breaks land before the file is saved. Do not treat it as final until the last page looks right.
Fix cut-off columns and blank pages in the PDF

Cut-off columns happen when the table is wider than the page. Work through the fixes in this order, and check the preview after each one. Start with the cheapest change and move on only if the table still does not fit.

items: Switch Orientation to the sideways option.
Choose a smaller margin preset, or type custom margins that are narrower.
Pick a larger Paper size if your printer setup supports it.
Select only the table with Selected cells, so the page holds no empty space.

blocks.text: Some guides mention Fit to width or Scale. Google's print help page does not list either setting, so check your own print window. If you see Fit to width, use it on wide tables. If you do not, the steps above are the reliable fallback.

Blank pages usually come from empty columns or rows far away from your data. Clear the extra formatting on those cells, or select only the cells you need and print Selected cells. The blank pages then drop out of the export.
When Download or Print is greyed out for viewers

The file owner controls this. In Google Drive, the owner opens Share, then clicks Settings, the gear icon. Under People who can download, copy, print, and access, separate checkboxes control Editors, Commenters, and Viewers. Clear the box for a role to block that role.

Google's Drive help page does not say whether Editors can download by default. Check the setting on your file rather than guessing. If you are a Viewer and the boxes block you, ask the owner to allow downloading and printing, or ask for Editor access. Neither fix requires changing the file itself.
File > Download versus File > Print

File > Download lets you choose a file type, and the file saves to your computer. Google's help page describes this path but gives no PDF layout steps. Some third-party guides show a PDF option in that menu. If you see it, it makes a quick copy.

For page setup, use File > Print. Paper size, orientation, margins, headers, page breaks, and repeated rows all live in the print settings. A quick download does not offer those controls, so use it only when the layout already looks right.
Keyboard shortcuts and the Mac print dialog

⌘P opens the Print window in Google Sheets. Google's keyboard shortcut page lists Print as ⌘P on Mac. Google lists no shortcut for Download or Save as PDF, so the save step is a click. For more shortcuts in Sheets, see [how to show keyboard shortcuts in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/show-keyboard-shortcuts-in-google-sheets).

In Chrome, the macOS print dialog may open after you click Print. Apple's Mac User Guide says you can click the PDF button at the bottom left and confirm the save, or use the PDF pop-up menu and choose Save as PDF. Command+P opens the Print dialog in Mac apps, the same key Sheets uses.
Export limits and file size for big spreadsheets

Google Drive's limits page says a spreadsheet in Google Sheets can hold up to 20 million cells or 100 MB. That is a file limit, not a PDF export limit. Google's export help page gives no separate PDF limit either.

A very large workbook can still take a while to prepare for print. If the full export feels stuck, try Current sheet first, then export the other tabs one at a time. Smaller exports are easier to check, and easier to fix when one setting is wrong.
Mistakes people make when they export Sheets to PDF

items: Exporting before selecting. Selected cells only matches the range you highlighted before you opened File > Print.
Skipping the preview. The preview shows cut-off columns and page breaks before you save.
Reading a greyed-out button as a bug. It is usually a sharing setting on the file.
Pressing ⌘P while another window is active. Make sure the Sheets tab is in front.
Saving the PDF without opening it. Open it in Preview once, so you catch problems before you send it.

blocks.text: Check the PDF before you send it

Open your Downloads folder in Finder, or check the download list in your browser. Open the PDF in Preview and scroll through every page. Look for cut-off columns, repeated headers, and page breaks in the wrong place.

Give the file a clear name when Chrome asks for one. A name that says what the report covers and when it was made saves you a search later. Keep the spreadsheet as the working copy, and export again when the data changes.
What to do next with your exported PDF

Messy data makes a messy PDF. Duplicate rows, stray blank rows, and mixed date formats all show up in the export. Clean the table first, then print it. For duplicates, see [remove duplicate rows in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/remove-duplicate-rows-in-google-sheets).

If the report needs a particular order, sort it before you print, because the PDF follows the order on screen. For sorting steps, see [sort data by column in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/sort-data-by-column-in-google-sheets).

faq.question: Is there a Google Sheets app for Mac?
faq.answer: No. Google Sheets on Mac runs in a browser at sheets.google.com. Chrome can install it as an app, but that app is still the web version, so the export steps stay the same.

faq.question: Can I export Google Sheets as PDF without using Print?
faq.answer: Some guides show a PDF option under File > Download. Google's help page describes Download without PDF layout steps, so check your own menu. For page setup and repeated headers, use File > Print.

faq.question: Why does my header row disappear on page two of the PDF?
faq.answer: The header row was not set to repeat. Freeze the top row in the sheet first, then open File > Print, turn on Repeat frozen rows or columns, and check the preview.

faq.question: Why is Download or Print greyed out for me?
faq.answer: The file owner has switched off downloading, printing, or copying for your role. Ask the owner to change the setting under Share > Settings, or ask for Editor access.

faq.question: Does Safari save the PDF without asking me?
faq.answer: Yes. Google says that in Firefox or Safari the PDF downloads automatically after you click Next. In Chrome, you click Print in the window that appears.

faq.question: Can I make the PDF fit the page width?
faq.answer: Some third-party guides mention Fit to width or Scale. Google's print help page does not list either option, so check your print window. If neither appears, use the orientation and margin fixes in this guide.

faq.question: Do I need Chrome to export a PDF on a Mac?
faq.answer: No. Safari and Firefox export a PDF too. Chrome adds one extra step, because it shows a Print window that you confirm before the file is saved.

steps.name: Open the file in your browser
steps.text: Go to sheets.google.com and open the spreadsheet in Chrome, Safari, or Firefox. Sheets on a Mac has no separate app, so the browser tab is where you export from.
steps.tip: Keep the Sheets tab in front. The keyboard shortcut works only in the active window.

steps.name: Select the cells or sheet tab
steps.text: To export one tab, click that tab at the bottom of the screen. To export one table, drag across its cells. Skip this step if you want the whole workbook.
steps.tip: Select before you open Print, so the Selected cells option matches your range.

steps.name: Open the Print window
steps.text: Click File in the menu bar at the top of the screen, then choose Print. You can also press ⌘P. The print settings open in the Sheets window.
steps.tip: If the window does not open, click the Sheets page once and try again.

steps.name: Choose what to print
steps.text: Under sheet options, choose Workbook, Selected cells, or Current sheet. Confirm the option you want is selected before you continue.
steps.tip: The table in this guide explains each option.

steps.name: Set paper size and orientation
steps.text: Open Paper size and pick the size you need, or choose Custom size for unusual paper. Under Orientation, pick the sideways option for tables that run across the page.
steps.tip: Choose Portrait for long, narrow lists.

steps.name: Set margins and headers
steps.text: Under Margins, pick a preset or choose Custom and type your numbers. Under Headers & footers, add the text you need. Use Edit custom fields to build your own.
steps.tip: Narrower margins give a wide table more room on the page.

steps.name: Set page breaks and repeated rows
steps.text: If the table runs onto a second page, drag the break lines to where you want them and select Confirm breaks. Turn on Repeat frozen rows or columns if you froze the header row.
steps.tip: Freeze the header row in the sheet before you open Print.

steps.name: Check the preview
steps.text: Scroll through the preview. Look for cut-off columns, blank pages, and rows that split in the wrong place. Change the setting, then check again.
steps.tip: Cut-off columns can still show up in the saved file, so check the PDF too.

steps.name: Click Next
steps.text: Click Next at the bottom of the print settings. In Chrome, a Print window appears, so click Print there. Firefox and Safari download the PDF right away.
steps.tip: Firefox and Safari skip the second window, so check your Downloads folder.

steps.name: Save the PDF in Chrome
steps.text: If the macOS print dialog opens, click the PDF button at the bottom left, then choose Save as PDF. Name the file, pick a folder, and click Save.
steps.tip: Read the labels rather than the layout, because the dialog can look different on other Macs.

steps.name: Find and check the file
steps.text: Open your Downloads folder in Finder, or check the download list in your browser. Open the PDF in Preview and scroll through it before you send it.
steps.tip: Open the PDF in Preview, not in a browser tab, to see the saved layout.

troubleshooting.problem: Download or Print is greyed out
troubleshooting.fix: You probably have Viewer or Commenter access, and the owner has switched the option off. Ask the owner to allow it under Share > Settings, or ask for Editor access.

troubleshooting.problem: Columns are cut off in the PDF
troubleshooting.fix: Switch Orientation to the sideways option, pick a smaller margin preset, or type narrower custom margins. If your print window shows Fit to width, use it. Then check the preview again.

troubleshooting.problem: The header row is missing on page two
troubleshooting.fix: Freeze the top row in the sheet first. Then open File > Print and turn on Repeat frozen rows or columns.

troubleshooting.problem: Blank pages at the end of the PDF
troubleshooting.fix: The range includes empty columns or rows far from the data. Select only the table, choose Selected cells, and print again.

troubleshooting.problem: The Mac dialog shows only a printer list
troubleshooting.fix: Click the PDF button at the bottom left, then choose Save as PDF. If you still see only printers, cancel and reopen the print window from Sheets.

troubleshooting.problem: The PDF shows the wrong sheet
troubleshooting.fix: Check the scope option. Current sheet prints only the open tab, while Workbook prints every tab in the file.
